source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Estric_2025_SetSettingTherapeuticSR.pdf, online-first version paginated 1-20 (anchors cite 'PDF p. N'). Abstract, Methods, Results, Discussion and declarations read from the text layer; Figure 1 and the landscape tables (Table 1 on pp. 5-6, Table 2 on p. 10, Table 3 on pp. 11-15) read on rotated renders at 150 and 200 dpi, with the mirrored text layer reversed as a cross-check. Table 2 ticks counted on the render; Table 1 sex and sample columns summed. No supplement.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim calls the review a mapping of what the trials reported, 'without appraising them or combining their outcomes', which is exactly what the paper did, and it attributes the preparation remark to the review rather than to evidence.
claims.note: 21, 19 and 18 of 25 are the printed Table 2 totals and agree with the text. 'Mostly one to four [meetings], of about 2 hours each' matches p. 8, where meetings of about 2 h are listed as one, two, three or four interviews (Gasser et al. 2014 appears under both one and two, so the per-number counts do not add to 19). The remark the claim questions reads that a preparatory phase of two interviews, the second the day before and lasting 5 h, maximized the psychedelic experience and the therapeutic effects (p. 8), citing a trial that compared psilocybin with escitalopram (Table 1, p. 5) and varied no preparation.

anchors.locator: Table 2, Total/25 row (counted on a rotated 200-dpi render)
anchors.extracted: Of 25 trials: information on psychedelic effects 21 (84%); therapeutic alliance meeting 19 (76%); advice on the attitude to adopt during the session 18 (72%). Participant selection items 25 (100%) each; specific monitor training the lowest at 13 (52%).

Oral or written information on psychedelic effects, side effects and study purpose was given in all trials except four where it is not mentioned (so 21). In 19 trials clinicians met participants beforehand to build trust and therapeutic alliance, meetings of about 2 h on days other than the session, listed as one, two, three or four interviews (one trial 3 h in total, one 6-8 h). Advice on how to behave was given at these meetings, most often to keep an open attitude and 'let go'. The paragraph also states that a two-interview preparatory phase, the second lasting 5 h the day before, maximized the psychedelic experience and the therapeutic effects (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021; Murphy et al., 2022).
The authors state that it is unclear how important context is for a therapeutic effect and that there are no studies comparing the efficacy of psychedelics in different sets and settings.

anchors.locator: Abstract; Methods > Data source and research strategy; Results > Study selection and Data extraction
anchors.extracted: 27 articles on 25 trials (13 randomized, 12 open-label) of classic psychedelics in psychiatric disorders, addiction treatment excluded; PubMed and Web of Science to 12 September 2022, rerun 6 December 2023 (the abstract says until 12 December 2023); because the review is descriptive, no data synthesis was planned and no risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of the trials is reported.

claims.note: '16 trials played a set playlist through headphones' is the review's own count; the two trials with no music are identifiable only in Table 3 (landscape page, read on the render).

anchors.extracted: Eleven trials asked participants to wear an eye mask throughout and one only to close their eyes. Sixteen trials played a predefined selection of music through headphones, described as relaxing and helping to let go, with the playlist available for several of them; in Holze et al. (2023) music alternated with silence, without headphones, with instruments such as drums or singing bowls possible at the therapist's wish.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (continued), Environment column, Dos Santos et al. (2021) and D'Souza et al. (2022) rows
anchors.extracted: Dos Santos et al. (2021): quiet, neutral room, reclining chair, mobile phone avoided, music and movies not allowed, reading allowed. D'Souza et al. (2022): typical hospital setting, medical-grade reclining chair, no music, no decoration, standard hospital lighting. These are the two trials in which no music was played.

The review excluded addiction treatment and studies using psychedelics for withdrawal, so trials in substance use disorders (such as a smoking-cessation pilot) were out of scope; and it reports no study comparing the efficacy of psychedelics in different sets and settings.

claims.overstatement: None. 'The trials were not appraised' and 'a choice the review's authors judged to have been made without evidence' both match the paper, the second being the review's own judgment rather than a finding.
claims.note: 'Five, published in 2023, one per participant' is the review's count on p. 17; it lists six citations because Lewis et al. 2023a and 2023b are one trial. Table 2 marks one monitor during the session for Holze, von Rotz, Goodwin 2023 and Sloshower, and four for the Lewis group trial (one therapist per patient).

anchors.locator: Results > Monitor training and presence during the session, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Twelve trials placed two monitors in the same room as the participant for the entire session, and one reported four monitors (D'Souza et al., 2022). One trial under COVID-19 had one monitor in the room and a second present virtually; in the group-therapy trial four therapists were present with four patients. Monitor gender was only occasionally specified.

Earlier trials routinely had two monitors per patient, but five of the trials published in 2023 used a single monitor per patient, which the authors relate to feasibility, human resources and cost (citing Goodwin 2023, Holze 2023, Lewis 2023a/b, Sloshower 2023, von Rotz 2023).

Two trends: disguising the hospital setting (living-room style in five trials; decorated, pleasant or peaceful in others; fresh flowers or plants) against making no particular change to the hospital environment in four trials (D'Souza 2022, Osorio 2015, Sanches 2016, Zeifman 2021); one room was described as designed for psychedelic drug administration. Furniture ranged from sofa or sofa-bed to bed or recliner; the group trial used an auditorium room with an infusion suite.

The decision to disguise the dosing room rather than simply make it more pleasant 'appears to have been taken arbitrarily, without evidence-based reasoning'; the authors say it would be interesting to test whether room decoration affects the therapeutic effect.
No studies compare the efficacy of psychedelics in different sets and settings; the review's only appraisal of the trials is the 16-item score for whether each feature was described.

key_findings.note: Figure 1 read on the render: 3,045 + 1,867 = 4,912; -1,282 (no English or French abstract) = 3,630; -3,322 (title) = 308; -71 (duplicates) = 237; -190 (abstract) = 47 full texts; -32 = 15, plus 12 after the update.

Counted the citations on p. 7: 13 trials excluding other illicit psychoactive substance use, 7 excluding alcohol dependence.
Editors' tallies re-counted and reproduced, including 13 trials for the two-week washout once Carhart-Harris 2021 and Murphy 2022 are counted as one.
Also noticed, not on the card: Gasser et al. (2014) is listed both among the trials with one preparatory interview and among those with two (p. 8).
The two no-music trials verified in Table 3 on p. 13.

All eleven named rows checked on the Table 3 renders and the reversed text layer (Moreno light snack, Grob and Palhano-Fontes light breakfast, Griffiths and Davis low-fat breakfast, Sloshower light breakfast, Goodwin 2022 light meal and fruit, Lewis light snacks and refreshments, Reckweg a meal provided, Aaronson a light meal shared at the end, Peck standardized breakfast introduced partway through).
Median 14, range 6-16, three trials at 16 (Carhart-Harris 2021/Murphy, Sloshower, Lewis); the ayahuasca and DMT trials hold the lowest totals (6 to 12).

reporting_issues.note: My own sum of Table 1 is 761, so the Results figure is the right one.
16 of 25 trials is 64%; psilocybin trials hold 596 of 761 participants (78%) by my sum. Nothing in the paper yields 47%.

I counted the column independently on the render: 21 ticks, the four blanks being Schneier 2023, Holze 2023, Goodwin 2023 and Reckweg 2023, against a printed 20 (80%). The printed column totals sum to 313 and the row totals to 314, as the card says. The neighbouring 'pleasant environment' column does have the printed 17.
Gasser 2014, 'private practice office' (p. 11) and Sloshower 2023, 'outpatient office' (p. 14), against 'All studies were conducted in a hospital facility' (p. 9).
The reference list (p. 19 in my copy, 19-20 across the columns) titles Reckweg's trial as a vaporized 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine formulation (GH001), while the text and Table 1 call it DMT.

Flagged as unsettled, which is right: Zeifman's Table 1 row has the same sex split as Sanches (14 women, 3 men) and refers to Sanches for adverse effects, but the review never says whether the samples overlap.

All four mismatches checked: two-thirds against 20 of 25 (80%); 'most studies insisted on two monitors of different genders' (p. 17) against 'occasionally specified' (p. 9); the 16-psilocybin list names Lewis twice and omits Aaronson 2023, which Table 1 has as psilocybin; '27 included studies' where 27 is the number of articles.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is right for a systematic review, and critically low follows from the unmet critical items (no protocol, restricted search, no list of excluded studies, no appraisal, risk of bias ignored in interpretation). Item 4 as 'no' is a defensible reading: the language restriction removed 1,282 records and is not justified.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it substantial rather than minor. The discussion concludes from five uncontrolled open-label reports that psychedelics have a therapeutic effect independent of context (p. 17), a causal reading the review's own design cannot support and that sits against its statement that no trial compared settings; the abstract also carries two figures that the Results contradict (763 participants, psilocybin 47%). The card documents all of this, so the difference is in the rating word only.

missed: Possible double counting in the pre-session paragraph (p. 8): Gasser et al. (2014) appears both among trials with one preparatory interview and among those with two, so the per-number lists do not add to the 19 trials stated in the same sentence.

The review contains no statement of who scored the 16 sub-domains or whether the scoring was duplicated, which the card records under exposure and AMSTAR item 6 but not as a reporting issue; it is the reason the Table 2 counts cannot be reproduced independently without re-reading all 27 articles.
